Please review the following manuscript. I'm really excited about this paper. My overall impression is excellent, and I'd be very happy to see it accepted.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

Here is the manuscript:

/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b05/review-experiment-rlgvkea8/call-e86fbe832c3b47c4ada131159d04e32b/manuscript.pdf

command_activity.command: /bin/bash -c 'ls -l manuscript.pdf && command -v pdftotext && command -v pdftoppm && command -v pdfinfo'
/bin/bash -c "python3 -c 'import importlib.util; print({m: bool(importlib.util.find_spec(m)) for m in [\"pypdf\", \"pdfplumber\", \"fitz\", \"PIL\"]})' "

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs && python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r = PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:', len(r.pages))
print('Metadata:', r.metadata)
texts = []
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages):
    t = p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
    texts.append(f'\\n--- PAGE {i+1} ---\\n{t}')
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n'.join(texts))
print('\\n'.join(texts[:3]))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
p = Path('tmp/pdfs')
for name in ['manuscript.txt'] + [f'page-{i:02d}.png' for i in range(1, 10)]:
    (p / name).unlink(missing_ok=True)
PY"

strengths: LPAM addresses a practical stitching problem: residual misalignment can prevent seam cutting from finding an acceptable boundary. Its training-free, modular design has potential value for existing panorama pipelines.

Table I reports consistent improvements across four seam-cutting methods and 79 image pairs from three datasets. For example, baseline SSIM on SEAGULL improves from 0.638 to 0.696. Figures 1, 5, and 6 also demonstrate visible structural repairs.

Constraining patch-boundary labels to preserve connections with the original seam is a sensible design. The overview, pseudocode, and intermediate visualizations make the overall procedure understandable.
The manuscript attributes its main computational components and existing datasets, provides a code/data link and several implementation settings, and candidly illustrates meaningful failure cases.
weaknesses: The distinctive contribution beyond existing seam-guided alignment is insufficiently established. Tables I–II compare seam cutters with and without additional alignment, but do not quantitatively compare against closely related alignment–seam methods such as [21] and SEAGULL [25]. Figure 6 provides only one qualitative comparison with Parallax and SEAGULL, leaving the proposed approach's comparative advantage uncertain.

The central flow modification is ambiguously specified. Equation (4) applies f to a displacement vector, whereas Equation (5) defines a scalar sigmoid whose argument is subsequently described as a normalized spatial coordinate. The intended operation, presumably spatial weighting of the flow, needs an explicit formula and treatment of different patch orientations and boundaries. The sigmoid also does not impose exact endpoint matching. These are potentially correctable presentation issues, but they currently obstruct reproduction of the main operation.

The evidence does not isolate the proposed design choices. Figure 3 examines several sigmoid settings on one example, but there are no dataset-level ablations of the seam detector, patch extent, or flow tapering against untapered flow and simpler weighting. Consequently, the experiments establish benefits from adding local alignment more clearly than benefits from the particular LPAM design.

The quantitative evaluation mainly measures agreement between image patches around the selected seam, with SSIM also driving patch selection. These measures are relevant but cannot adequately establish preservation of scene geometry or absence of new artifacts elsewhere in repaired patches. Independent perceptual or distortion assessment and per-image improvement/degradation rates would substantially strengthen the visual-quality claim.

The operating assumptions materially restrict robustness. The max(Q) ≤ 1.5·mean(Q) test accepts uniformly poor seams, while cropping does not ensure that occluded pixels have valid correspondences as assumed in Equation (3). Figure 7 acknowledges detection and merging failures, but their frequency is unreported. Thus, the assertion that false-positive patches cannot yield inferior results is unsupported.

Generality and efficiency are only partially demonstrated: all quantitative experiments use REW prealignment, and LPAM adds approximately 7–10 seconds to seam cutters that often take 3.5–10 seconds themselves. Input resolutions and end-to-end timing comparisons with competing seam-guided alignment methods are missing, limiting assessment of the quality–cost tradeoff.
